blog_articles.page_title: How Can Self Storage Help During a Kitchen Renovation?
paragraphs: Kitchen renovations are exciting to imagine, but the reality of the process is often extremely demanding. Between dust, displaced appliances, and contractors navigating your home, the chaos can quickly overwhelm even the most organized homeowner.

Self storage helps during a kitchen renovation by moving furniture, appliances, cookware, and other household items out of the work area. A storage unit gives contractors more room to work and helps keep your temporary living space organized.

Use self storage before a kitchen remodel to clear countertops, cabinets, dining areas, and nearby rooms. Store items you do not need during the project, then keep only daily-use essentials available at home.
If you’re planning a kitchen remodel, here are some practical solutions that can save you time, stress, and money.

Put items in storage when they take up space in or near the kitchen and you do not need them for your temporary daily routine. This includes counter stools, dining furniture, extra dishes, specialty cookware, small appliances, kitchen décor, and boxes from cabinets or pantries.

Start by packing the items you use least often. Store serving platters, baking tools, extra glassware, countertop appliances, seasonal décor, and duplicate kitchen supplies before packing everyday dishes and utensils.
Store only the items you plan to use again after the renovation. Declutter before packing so you do not move unnecessary items back into the updated kitchen.

Storage creates more open space for contractors, materials, tools, and renovation work. Clearing furniture, boxes, appliances, and kitchen items out of the work area reduces obstacles and helps contractors move through the space more easily.

Move dining furniture, counter stools, appliances, and nearby décor out before demolition or construction begins. This gives your renovation team access to cabinets, walls, flooring, and work surfaces without navigating around household items.

A storage unit also helps keep the rest of your home more functional. Instead of moving kitchen items into bedrooms, hallways, garages, or living areas, organize them in one storage space until the project is complete.

Choose a storage unit size based on the number of boxes, appliances, furniture pieces, and dining-area items you plan to store. A 5×5 or 5×10 unit often fits boxes, small appliances, cookware, counter stools, and compact furniture from a kitchen renovation.

Choose

paragraphs: The best choice depends on your moving distance, home size, budget, timeline, and ability to handle heavy lifting. Professional movers offer convenience and efficiency, while DIY moving can cost less but requires more time and physical effort. For many moves, a hybrid approach—packing yourself and hiring movers for loading and transportation—offers a practical middle ground.

Professional movers can be worth the additional cost if you have a large household, heavy furniture, or limited time. Experienced crews can handle packing, loading, transportation, and unloading, reducing the amount of physical work you need to do.

A local professional move may cost approximately $1,000–$2,500, while a long-distance move can cost $2,000–$5,000 or more. Actual prices vary based on factors such as the distance, number of belongings, labor required, moving date, packing services, and other services or fees.
Get multiple estimates and compare what each quote includes before choosing a moving company.
A DIY move can be a cost-effective option if you’re moving a small amount of furniture, staying relatively close to home, and having friends or family available to help.

A DIY move may start with approximately $150–$500 for a rental truck, but the total cost can be higher after adding fuel, mileage, packing materials, moving equipment, insurance, tolls, and food for helpers.

Before choosing DIY, calculate the 
total estimated cost
, not just the truck rental price.

Choose professional movers if:
You have a large or long-distance move, a tight schedule, heavy furniture, valuable belongings, or limited ability to handle the physical work.

Choose DIY if:
You’re moving to a small household locally, have plenty of time, want maximum control, and have enough help to safely move your belongings.

Choose a hybrid move if:
You want to save money by packing yourself but need help with loading, transportation, unloading, or particularly heavy items.
You don’t necessarily have to choose between doing everything yourself and hiring a full-service moving company. A hybrid move lets you handle some tasks while paying professionals for others.
This approach can help reduce labor costs while making the most physically demanding parts of the move easier.

The key to using 2026’s colors is balance. Start with a neutral base on the main walls, then add bolder hues through accent walls, doors, or built-in shelving. This lets you refresh your look without overwhelming a space.

blog_articles.page_title: How to Adjust When Moving From a Large Space to a Small Space
paragraphs: Adjusting from a large home to a smaller space is difficult, but can be done if you choose items to take with you with discernment, store items not needed often, and part with items that are not useful. If you make a plan before you move, sort items before packing, and use storage strategically, you can create a functional home without crowding every closet, corner, and walkway.

Moving into a smaller home, apartment, condo, or townhouse often requires a different approach to furniture, décor, clothing, and household supplies. Focus on what supports your daily routine, then donate, recycle, gift, store, or put away the rest.

Determining what supports your daily routine helps you decide what belongs in your smaller home.
 Start with the items you use regularly, such as daily clothing, kitchen supplies, work materials, seating, and bedroom furniture.

Focus first on the belongings that support daily life; a smaller space works best when it reflects your current routine. Don’t attempt to stuff everything from your previous home into a smaller space; clutter makes a small space feel even smaller.

Reducing the number of items to be moved before packing reduces the number of boxes, furniture pieces, and household items you move.
 Work through one room at a time, and avoid shifting clutter from one area to another.

This culling process helps create a clearer inventory before moving day. It also gives you time to pack more intentionally instead of bringing every item into a smaller home and sorting later; it’s easier to add to your new home thoughtfully than to have to continue to remove items.

Mapping the new layout before moving helps you determine which furniture and belongings will fit in your smaller space.
 Request a floor plan, take measurements during a walkthrough, or measure rooms after you receive access to the new home. Then measure doorways, stairwells, elevators, hallways, and room dimensions. Compare those measurements with each furniture piece before moving it.
Consider each piece and what function(s) it serves; multipurpose items are very useful when working with a small space.
Keeping doors, walkways, and frequently used areas clear makes a smaller home easier to use.

Using vertical and closed storage helps you organize a smaller home without filling floors and surfaces with clutter.
 Tall bookcases, wall-mounted cabinets, floating shelves, hooks, and pegboards use wall space while keeping walkways open.

Closed storage helps contain smaller household items, while open shelving creates room for books, décor, and daily-use supplies. A combination of both adds structure without removing personality from your space.

Using self-storage unit for items that do not fit your smaller living space helps you keep your home focused on your everyday routine and avoid unneeded clutter.
 Pack away seasonal clothing and décor, extra furniture, rarely used hobby equipment, and other household items you plan to use later or do not need on a regular basis.

A self-storage unit gives you extra room without forcing immediate decisions about what to do with everything you own. Store items you want to rotate back into your home as your needs, hobbies, or seasons change, or even to keep items that you haven’t decided if you want to keep or not; consider keeping a space of the unit that is reserved for items you’re still considering.

Public Storage Size Guide
 to compare unit sizes.

For interstate moves, confirm that the mover or broker is registered and review its complaint history before booking.
Start researching movers as soon as your moving date is reasonably firm.
May through September is the busy moving season, so availability may be more limited during those months.
There is no universal rule that you must book exactly six or eight weeks ahead. Your timeline will depend on location, season, move distance and mover availability.
For an interstate move, check the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s mover database to confirm that the mover or broker is registered and has a U.S. DOT number.
For an in-state move, requirements may differ, so check your state or local consumer-protection or transportation agency.
That distinction matters because a broker does not necessarily transport your belongings itself. Interstate household-goods brokers must be registered and use registered movers.

When comparing estimates, look at more than the total price.

valuation coverage

blog_articles.page_title: How Do You Stage a Home to Sell?
paragraphs: Stage a home to sell by decluttering, depersonalizing, cleaning, completing minor repairs, improving lighting, and arranging furniture to show each room’s function. The goal is to help buyers evaluate the home’s layout, storage, condition, and potential during listing photos and showings.

Start with high-visibility areas such as the entryway, kitchen, living room, bathrooms, bedrooms, closets, and exterior. Pack away extra furniture and household items early so you can keep the home organized while it is listed.
Here’s everything you need to know about staging a home to help it sell.

Home staging is the process of preparing a house, condo, or apartment for listing photos, open houses, and buyer showings. Unlike decorating for personal use, staging focuses on making the home’s features, layout, and condition easier for buyers to understand.
Staging can include packing away personal belongings, reducing furniture, cleaning surfaces, making repairs, and giving each room one clear purpose.
Yes. Decluttering before selling helps buyers see room size, storage capacity, natural light, and walkways more clearly. It also gives you a head start on packing for your move.
Do not move clutter from visible rooms into closets or cabinets. Buyers may open storage areas during a showing.
Yes. Depersonalizing helps buyers focus on the home rather than the current household. Pack away family photos, children’s artwork, refrigerator papers, highly personal décor, and excess accessories.
Leave enough simple décor to show how a room can function. The goal is a home that feels welcoming without making buyers feel like they are walking through someone else’s personal space.

Talk to a real estate agent before staging to identify the projects that fit your local market and home type. An agent can help you prioritize repairs, paint, furniture changes, curb appeal, and other updates before listing.
Ask which projects buyers in your area notice most and whether a specific update fits comparable homes currently for sale.
Low-cost home staging focuses on cleaning, decluttering, lighting, minor repairs, and furniture arrangement. These updates can improve the home’s presentation without requiring a full remodel.

Paint before selling when walls are visibly worn, marked, or painted in highly specific colors. Light, neutral colors can make rooms feel brighter and help buyers focus on the home’s layout and features.
You do not need to repaint every room automatically. Ask your real estate agent which spaces would benefit most before adding painting to the listing plan.

blog_articles.page_title: Is It Better to Rent or Buy a Home?
paragraphs: Whether it is better to rent or buy depends on your budget, savings, expected length of stay, local housing costs, and preferred level of flexibility. Renting can work well when you expect your location, job, or household needs to change. Buying can work well when you have a stable plan, funds for upfront and ongoing costs, and a long-term interest in a specific home or area.

Compare the full cost of renting with the full cost of owning before deciding. Include upfront costs, monthly payments, taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, parking, HOA fees, and moving expenses—not only rent and mortgage payments.

The main difference between renting and buying is that renters pay to live in a home for a set lease period, while homeowners purchase a property and manage its costs, maintenance, and long-term decisions.
Renting can make it easier to relocate for work, school, family changes, or a different neighborhood. Buying can provide more control over the home’s layout, finishes, storage, and long-term use.
Neither option is automatically better. The right choice depends on what fits your finances and routine now.

You may be financially ready to buy when you have funds for upfront costs, a monthly budget that supports total ownership expenses, and an emergency fund separate from your home-buying savings. Mortgage approval also depends on income, debt, credit history, loan program, down payment, and property details.
A lender can explain loan programs, estimated payments, and the financial information used during the mortgage process.

Buying may make more sense when you expect to stay in the home or area for several years. Purchasing and selling a home can involve closing costs, moving costs, commissions, repairs, and other expenses that may be harder to recover during a short stay.
The exact rent-versus-buy break-even point varies by market, loan terms, property taxes, rent trends, and future sale conditions.

Local housing costs can change the rent-versus-buy decision. Home prices, rent, property taxes, insurance, HOA fees, maintenance costs, parking, and transportation costs vary by neighborhood and property type.
Compare similar homes whenever possible. For example, compare the monthly rent for a two-bedroom apartment with the estimated ownership cost of a similar two-bedroom condo or house in the same area.

Use current local listings and professional guidance to evaluate a specific market. Rent-versus-buy calculators can organize estimates, but they cannot predict future home prices, rents, or mortgage rates.

Lifestyle factors can determine whether renting or buying fits your daily routine. Renting can support a flexible lifestyle with fewer home-maintenance tasks. Buying can support households that want more control over the home’s layout, paint colors, storage, landscaping, or future updates.
Both renting and buying can support different stages of life. Focus on the option that works for your current plans rather than choosing based on a general rule.

Label boxes by owner so nothing gets lost in the shuffle. Store seasonal items in clear bins for easy rotation, and use shelving to make the most of vertical space. Leave a walkway in the middle so you can grab things without unpacking the whole unit.
Combining households is easier when you’re not surrounded by clutter. Using a storage unit creates space for new routines and memories while keeping your belongings accessible.

blog_articles.page_title: 22 Tips for Packing and Organizing Your Storage Unit
paragraphs: Storage unit organization is actually both an art and a science.
Solid storage unit organization will help you know exactly where you put each item so that it will not be hard to retrieve later. That way, you don’t have to open every box just to find one item.

“If you have items that have been in a storage unit for a while, you can easily forget what is in them,” says Sabrina M. Quairoli of 
Sabrina’s Organizing & Admin Services.
More importantly, packing thoughtfully and organizing your things can make them last longer.
If you have offsite storage, taking the time to organize and properly pack your things will prevent your stacks of boxes from falling over and possibly hurting you or damaging your other possessions.
Here are 22 tips to help ensure storage unit organization success for your self storage rental.
1. Plan ahead: Make a general plan of how you will place the boxes and furniture inside your storage unit before you get started.

2. Pallet the ground: Before putting the boxes in, arrange raised pallets according to your plan. Be sure to also clean the storage area thoroughly, as storage unit organization should start with a (clean) blank slate!
3. Avoid mildew: Refrain from putting in wet items as these may invite mildew, mold, and other types of water damage.

4. Make a list for logical storage unit organization: Quairoli recommends “writing down the content that is in each box on a spreadsheet like Evernote, OneNote, or Google Sheets. All you need is two columns, one with the ‘Box Number’ and one column for the ‘Content in Box’ items. When away from the storage unit, this file helps trigger your memory of what each box contains.” Then, you can easily share it with family members who are authorized to have access to the storage unit.

Is climate controlled storage for you? Read up on our guide to understanding 
climate controlled storage units.
5. Use shelves for storage: If there are shelves available, make use of them! Store smaller items or things you would like to keep handy.
6. Store smart: Store mirrors and frames standing on end, never flat.

7. Maintain accessibility: When it comes to storage unit organization, don’t store stacks and stacks of boxes together. Make an aisle that will allow you to get to a box without having to move anything out of the way.

blog_articles.page_title: Are Microtrends Making Your Closet More Cluttered?
paragraphs: One month, everyone wants leopard print. The next, it is ballet flats, cherry red, or a specific jacket style you suddenly see everywhere. Fashion has always moved in cycles, but social media can make those cycles feel faster than ever.

These short-lived aesthetics and must-have items are often called microtrends. They can be a fun way to experiment with personal style, but constantly cycling through new looks can also leave behind a closet full of clothes you no longer wear.

A microtrend is a fashion trend that rises in popularity quickly and may fade just as fast. Unlike broader trends that can influence fashion for several seasons or years, microtrends can seem to appear overnight.
Social media can accelerate that process. An outfit, shoe, or accessory starts appearing across your feed, gets recreated by countless people, and suddenly feels like something everyone owns.
The problem is that by the time you buy into one microtrend, another may already be taking its place.

Microtrends can create closet clutter because they encourage frequent wardrobe updates. Instead of slowly adding pieces you genuinely like, it can become easy to accumulate clothes based on what feels exciting at a particular moment.
Individual purchases may not seem significant. Over time, those pieces can add up.
Before adding a trending piece to your wardrobe, imagine it without the trend attached to it.

You do not have to avoid trends altogether. The goal is to separate 
“I like this”
 from 
“I keep seeing this.”

Waiting a few days or weeks before purchasing can help. If you are still thinking about the item after the initial excitement wears off, it may have a better chance of becoming part of your regular wardrobe.
Yes. Before shopping, take another look at what you already own.

Fashion trends repeat, which means the “new” look appearing online may already be hiding somewhere in your closet. An older cardigan, pair of boots, belt, or jacket might feel current again when styled differently.
The idea is not to stop having fun with fashion. It is to make trends work with your wardrobe instead of letting them take it over.

If you no longer like an item, consider donating, selling, or swapping it while it is still wearable. If you genuinely love something and are only putting it away because it is not currently trending, you do not have to get rid of it.

blog_articles.page_title: How Can You Make More Room in a Small NYC Apartment?
paragraphs: Small NYC apartments feel more organized when everyday items stay within reach and lower-use belongings do not crowd floors, counters, closets, or under-bed areas. Start with one small space, sort every item into a clear category, and return only what supports your current routine.
Whether you live in a studio, one-bedroom apartment, walk-up, co-op, condo, or shared space, a focused decluttering plan can create more room for daily life.
Start with the area that creates the most daily frustration. For many NYC apartment residents, that is the entryway, kitchen counter, closet floor, or area under the bed.
Set a timer for 30 minutes and choose one category, such as shoes, cookware, papers, or clothing. Remove every item from that category, then decide where it belongs before putting anything back.
Avoid creating a “decide later” pile. That pile often becomes clutter in a new location.
Floor space makes a small apartment feel larger and easier to use. Before purchasing shelves, bins, or furniture, remove items that do not need to stay on the floor.

After clearing the floor, use vertical space with wall hooks, shelving, over-the-door organizers, and stackable bins. Keep walkways open, especially between the entryway, kitchen, bathroom, bed, and closet.

Bulky belongings often take up more room than expected in a studio apartment. Furniture, luggage, extra bedding, seasonal wardrobes, and duplicate kitchen items can quickly reduce usable living space.
Look closely at items you own in multiples. You may not need several dish sets, extra lamps, unused furniture, or clothing that no longer fits your current lifestyle.
Keep the items that support your daily routine. Donate usable duplicates, then put away items you want to keep but do not use often.

NYC renters create more room when each area has one purpose. Your entryway should hold the items you use when leaving home. Your closet should hold the clothing you wear now. Your kitchen should hold the tools you use to prepare meals.

Small apartments are common throughout New York City, from Manhattan and Brooklyn to Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island. Whether you live in a studio on the Upper West Side, a walk-up in Harlem, or an apartment in Williamsburg, Long Island City, or Astoria, the same approach can help: keep daily-use items accessible, rotate seasonal belongings, and clear floor space before adding organizers.
Seasonal clothing and décor can take up valuable closet, cabinet, and under-bed space. Rotate these items instead of trying to keep every season accessible at once.
Keep current-season clothing at eye level and within easy reach. Put away sweaters, coats, holiday décor, or other out-of-rotation belongings in labeled containers.

blog_articles.page_title: How Do I Reset My Home After the Holidays?
paragraphs: After weeks of decorating, cooking, entertaining, and exchanging gifts, your home may need a little attention. Start by putting away your holiday decorations, cleaning up after holiday meals, and getting rid of clutter that accumulated during the season. Then, take a fresh look at your everyday belongings and decide what you actually want to keep.

Start by taking down your holiday decorations and sorting them before you put them away. Don’t automatically pack everything back into the same boxes. If something is broken, worn out, or you didn’t enjoy using it this year, decide whether it’s worth keeping.
Clean decorations before storing them, especially anything that collected dust or food residue during the holidays. Wrap fragile ornaments individually and keep similar decorations together.
Label each box with what’s inside so you won’t have to open several containers next year to find what you’re looking for.

If you have a real Christmas tree, check with your local city or county sanitation, public works, or environmental services department to see if there is a recycling or Christmas tree collection program. Many communities offer designated drop-off locations or curbside pickup after the holidays.

Remove all ornaments, lights, hooks, and other decorations before getting rid of the tree. Even if you don’t want them anymore, your tree may not be disposed of or recycled if it isn’t just tree and nothing else.
Don’t leave a dried-out tree inside your home for an extended period because it can become a fire hazard.

Remove ornaments and lights, disassemble the tree according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and take the time to clean off your artificial tree before putting it away. Wipe the limbs with a damp cloth to get rid of dust and lint they may have collected over the season. Let them dry and store the pieces in a container or bag that protects them from dust.
If the original box is damaged or difficult to use, consider replacing it with a sturdier storage container designed for artificial trees.

Once the decorations are down, use the empty surfaces as an opportunity to deep clean. Dust shelves, ceiling fans, light fixtures, and other areas that may have been overlooked during your regular cleaning routine.
You don’t have to tackle the entire house in one day. Work through one room at a time so the cleanup doesn’t become another overwhelming task.

The kitchen often needs extra attention after holiday cooking and entertaining. Start with the refrigerator and freezer. Throw away leftovers that have been sitting for several days and check expiration dates on other foods. Be sure to wipe down shelves and drawers while you have less food in the refrigerator.
Then clean your countertops, cabinets, oven, microwave, and other appliances that got extra use during the holidays.

Check your pantry and cupboards, too. If you bought specialty ingredients for holiday recipes that you aren’t likely to use again, consider whether you really need to keep them. When in doubt, check the expiration date. Will it last until next year?

blog_articles.page_title: How Do You Declutter a Closet in Orlando?
paragraphs: Declutter a closet in Orlando by sorting one clothing category at a time, keeping everyday items within reach, and putting away lower-use clothing, linens, and seasonal items. A clear keep, donate, recycle, or pack-away plan helps you create more room without buying organizers first.

Closet space fills quickly in homes and apartments across the Orlando area, from Downtown Orlando and College Park to Lake Nona, Dr. Phillips, Waterford Lakes, and East Orlando. Keep your main closet focused on the clothing, shoes, and linens you use most often, then put away items outside your current routine.
Start small. Choose one category, such as shoes, tops, handbags, or linens, instead of pulling everything out at once.
Return only the items that belong in your current closet. This approach keeps the task focused and gives you quick progress.
Keep clothing that fits, feels comfortable, and works for your present lifestyle. Place these items where you can see and reach them easily.
You may want to donate clothing that is still usable but no longer suits your size, work needs, style, or routine. Recycle or properly dispose of damaged items that cannot be reused.
Organize a crowded closet by category first: tops, pants, dresses, shoes, bags, and accessories. Then arrange each category by frequency of use.
Avoid buying more organizers until you finish decluttering. A closet often feels crowded because it holds too many items, not because it lacks containers.

Orlando wardrobes often include warm-weather clothing, travel items, special-occasion outfits, and layers for occasional cooler days. A regular closet reset helps keep the items you wear most often within reach while reducing crowded shelves and overfilled hanging rods.

Keep your daily clothing in the main closet, then put away less-used clothing as your needs change. Pack fully clean and dry travel layers, formalwear, cooler-weather clothing, and seasonal accessories in labeled containers.
This system gives your everyday wardrobe more space and makes seasonal changes easier.

Extra linens, seasonal décor, luggage, and clothing outside your current rotation can fill closet shelves before daily essentials have a place. Put away the items you want to keep but do not need right now.

climate-controlled storage
 available at select locations. Compare nearby Orlando locations to confirm current unit sizes, features, pricing, and access hours.

 provides a more consistent indoor environment for clothing, furniture, books, photographs, electronics, and décor affected by Orlando heat, high humidity, frequent rain, and tropical weather.

blog_articles.page_title: How Do You Store Camping Gear?
paragraphs: Store camping gear clean, dry, and organized by category. Use labeled bins or pouches, keep frequently used items accessible, and maintain a checklist so you’re ready for your next trip.
Use small pouches for accessories like repair kits, headlamps, matches, and charging cables.
If bulky camping equipment is taking over your home, a self-storage unit may provide extra room between trips.
Shake out debris, air-dry all components completely, clean zippers and seams, and store according to manufacturer instructions. A breathable storage sack may be preferable for long-term storage.

Make sure the bag is fully dry. Follow the manufacturer’s storage guidance; many sleeping bags should not remain tightly compressed between trips. Keep them in a clean, dry space away from direct sunlight.
Yes. A storage unit can be useful for clean, dry, seasonal items such as:
Check the facility’s rules before storing propane, fuel, chemicals, or other hazardous materials.

Can camping gear be stored in a garage?
Yes, if the garage is dry and protected from pests. Keep moisture-sensitive items off the floor.

Can you store a damp tent?
No. Always dry tents completely before packing them away.

Should sleeping bags be stored compressed?
It depends on the bag and manufacturer guidance. Many are best stored loosely for extended periods.

What should not be left in camping bins?
Food, trash, wet clothing, damp towels, and improperly stored fuel or hazardous materials.

How often should gear be inspected?
After every trip and before major outings.

Keeping camping gear clean, dry, and organized makes packing faster and helps protect your equipment. If gear is crowding your home, Public Storage may provide additional space for belongings you do not use every day.

blog_articles.page_title: How Do I Declutter a Spare Room for Holiday Guests?
paragraphs: Declutter a spare room for holiday guests by removing non-guest items, sorting belongings into clear categories, and setting up space for sleeping, luggage, clothing, and personal items. Use self storage for furniture, boxes, office supplies, craft materials, and household overflow that do not fit your guest-room setup.

Many spare rooms serve as home offices, hobby rooms, storage areas, or a combination of all three between visits. Start early, work through one category at a time, and keep only the furniture and supplies your guests will use.

Start decluttering a guest room by removing everything except the furniture guests will use. Clear boxes, office supplies, craft materials, clothing, décor, and household overflow from the room so you can see how much usable space remains.
Complete the sorting process before reorganizing the room. This prevents items from moving from one pile to another without creating more usable guest space.

Put away items that limit guest space or make the room feel crowded. This often includes personal clothing, storage bins, unopened boxes, office supplies, hobby materials, extra furniture, and seasonal décor that does not support the guest-room setup.
Guests need a clear place to sleep, set down luggage, hang clothing, and keep personal items. Clear a closet section, dresser drawer, shelf, or luggage area before arrival.
Keep the room simple. A made bed, clean surfaces, accessible lighting, fresh towels, and a place for belongings create a more useful guest space than adding extra décor or furniture.

Sort guest-room clutter by deciding what each item needs next. Donate or sell usable items that no longer fit your routine. Recycle or discard items that are damaged or no longer useful. Put away items that belong elsewhere in your home.

Use storage for furniture, boxes, household décor, hobby supplies, and other items you plan to use again but do not need in the guest room. A storage unit gives you time to decide what belongs in your home without leaving items stacked in a bedroom, closet, or hallway.
Handle donation, recycling, and discard items promptly. Move donation items to your car, schedule a pickup, or take them to a local drop-off location so they do not become a new pile in the house.

Keep a guest room ready between visits by giving it one primary purpose and using flexible furniture for any secondary use. A daybed, sleeper sofa, folding desk, storage bench, or filing cabinet can help the room function as both a guest room and a home office, reading room, or hobby area.

Use labeled bins or drawers for guest linens, towels, toiletries, and extra pillows. Keep one basic set of guest essentials in the room, then store duplicate bedding, extra furniture, and occasional-use supplies elsewhere.
A quick reset after each visit keeps the room ready for the next guest. Wash linens, restock towels and toiletries, clear surfaces, and return non-guest items to their designated storage areas.

Create guest storage by clearing a drawer, closet section, shelf, luggage stand, or storage bench. Guests need a place to put clothing, bags, toiletries, and small personal items without leaving everything on the floor or bed.

blog_articles.page_title: What Is the Best Way to Organize a Storage Unit?
paragraphs: The best way to organize a storage unit is to create an inventory, label every container, group belongings by category, and keep frequently used items easy to reach. A clear layout helps you use available space efficiently and find what you need without unpacking the entire unit.

Use storage zones, stable box stacks, freestanding shelving, and a walkway when unit size allows. Organizing before move-in makes it easier to access furniture, boxes, seasonal items, sports gear, business supplies, and household overflow throughout your rental.
Create an inventory before moving belongings into storage. List each box or bin number, general contents, storage category, and approximate location within the unit.
Keep the inventory in a phone note, spreadsheet, or document you can access before visiting the unit. An inventory helps you find a specific box without opening multiple containers.

For example, an inventory entry could read: 
Box 12 — Kitchen serving supplies — left shelving unit.
Use sturdy boxes or containers that stack without becoming unstable. Similar container sizes make it easier to organize rows, use vertical space, and keep labels visible.
Choose containers based on what you are storing. Use smaller boxes for heavier items, such as books or tools, and larger boxes for lightweight items, such as linens, pillows, and seasonal décor.
Label every box or bin with both a general category and specific contents. A detailed label makes it easier to identify what is inside without opening the container.
Place labels on at least two sides of each container. This keeps labels visible when boxes are stacked or placed on shelving.
Create storage zones by grouping similar belongings together. Separate furniture, clothing, seasonal décor, sports gear, business supplies, and household boxes into designated areas of the unit.
Use a simple diagram or photo of the layout if you manage a larger storage unit. This makes it easier to return items to the right area after a visit.

Leave a walkway through your storage unit when you expect to retrieve belongings during the rental period. A clear path from the entrance to the back wall helps you reach boxes, furniture, and shelves without moving everything in front of them.
Keep frequently used items along the walkway or near the entrance. Place less-used boxes, seasonal items, and larger furniture toward the back or along the walls.
Choose a unit size that fits your belongings and your access needs. The Public Storage Size Guide helps you compare storage-unit dimensions and approximate capacities before reserving.

blog_articles.page_title: How to Organize Your Bathroom Vanity
paragraphs: The best way to keep your bathroom vanity organized is to remove as much clutter as possible. Utilize vertical storage, dental organizers, medicine cabinets, floating shelves, and rolling carts to give you more storage.
Before you start to organize, do a thorough cleanout. Here’s what to do:
Vertical storage is the best way to organize your vanity without making it cluttered. There are several ways to do this.

A two- or three-tiered rotating organizer can sit beside your vanity and hold dozens of products. These organizers come in a lot of different styles, so you’re sure to find one that matches your bathroom.

If you only have a mirror over your sink, consider replacing it with a medicine cabinet. You’ll still have a mirror, plus storage behind it. This is a great place to hide away clutter. Some medicine cabinets are designed to be embedded between the studs on your wall, but others can be hung from a few screws. Make sure to check which one you’re getting before you buy.
If there’s room, you can also add small shelves around your mirror. Look for floating shelves that don’t stick too far out from the wall.

You can expand your vanity space with just a simple tweak. Get a three-tiered cart that’s the same height as your vanity and wheel it right next to it. The cart is the perfect place to put hair dryers, curling and straightening irons, makeup, hair products, and lotion. Put your less-used items on the lower shelves and items you use regularly on the top.
Measure the space where you want to put the cart before you buy one to ensure a good fit.

blog_articles.page_title: How to Organize Your Dishwasher for the Cleanest Dishes
paragraphs: The best way to organize your dishwasher for clean dishes is to leave space between items, face dishes toward the middle, keep tall items from blocking the spray arms, and put delicate items on the top rack. Turn bowls, cups, measuring cups, and other concave items upside down so water can drain, and make sure nothing blocks the soap dispenser or spray arms.

How you load your dishwasher can make a big difference in how well it cleans. Overloading the racks, nesting dishes together, or placing a pan where it blocks the spray can leave food and residue behind. A few simple changes can help water and detergent reach more of your dishes during each cycle.

Make sure to never put large pans flat against the door of the dishwasher. This can block the detergent and rinse agent from dispersing throughout the dishwasher and reaching all the dishes. Your best bet is to put plates in the area right in front of the door. Make sure they are placed between the tines, vertically towards the door instead of horizontally to it.

If the water can’t reach the dishes, they won’t get clean. It’s important to leave gaps between your dishes, especially plates and sheet pans. Don’t nest bowls and cups, and don’t let spoons and forks stick together.
Face all of your dishes towards the middle of the rack. This will give them the full force of the spray, making them cleaner.
Baking sheets and pots can be tall enough to block the spray arms of your dishwasher. If they don’t spin properly, then all of your dishes won’t get clean.

Some dishwashers have a side area meant to accommodate taller baking pans. You’ll notice a little part on the bottom of the second rack that’s raised to make room. This is where you’ll want to put tall, flat pans like pizza pans, cookie sheets, and baking pans.
When in doubt, spin the spray arm to see if it hits anything. If it does, you may need to wash that pan by hand.

Pots, pans, plates, and silverware can handle the heat and harder spray that the bottom rack provides. Things like plastic cups, glassware, and baby bottles should be put on the second rack. This gives you more room for harder-to-clean items on the bottom rack and prevents damage.
If an item is concave, turn it bowl-side down. This goes for ladles, serving spoons, measuring cups, and, of course, bowls.

If you put it on its side or right-side-up, it can fill with water and not drain. Then you’ll be left with a dishwasher soup of suds and food particles you’ll need to wash away when the cycle is over.

Ever unload your cutlery and find food gunk still stuck to it? The best way to ensure your cutlery gets clean is to put it in the silverware basket with the handles down, facing the bottom of the basket.
The only exceptions to the rule are butter and steak knives. Put those with the tip down so they don’t poke your hand when you’re unloading the dishwasher.

blog_articles.page_title: What Are the Best Alternatives to a Grass Lawn?
paragraphs: The best alternatives to a grass lawn include xeriscaping, ground covers, native grasses, wildflower gardens, hardscaping, decorative gravel, artificial turf, rain gardens, and raised garden beds. The best fit for your yard depends on local climate, rainfall, sun exposure, soil, drainage, foot traffic, maintenance preferences, and how you plan to use the space.
Replacing all or part of a traditional lawn can reduce mowing. Depending on the plants and materials you choose, it may also reduce supplemental watering and routine upkeep.

Xeriscaping is a landscaping approach designed to reduce or eliminate the need for supplemental irrigation that combines water-efficient plants, soil preparation, mulch, efficient irrigation when needed, and materials such as gravel or stone. While xeriscaping is often associated with dry climates, its water-conscious approach can be adapted to many regions. The key is selecting native or climate-appropriate plants that suit your yard’s conditions.

Ground cover plants are a useful grass alternative if you want greenery without a traditional turf lawn. Depending on your location and growing conditions, options may include clover, creeping thyme, moss, and other low-growing plants. Some ground covers can handle light foot traffic, but results vary by plant type, sunlight, soil, moisture, and climate. A local nursery or extension service can help identify plants that fit your region.

Native grasses and wildflower gardens often replace part of a lawn with a more natural-looking landscape. Once established, plants adapted to local conditions may require less supplemental water and maintenance than conventional turfgrass. Native vegetation may also provide food and habitat for pollinators and other wildlife.
Pro Tip: Look for seed mixes and plants recommended for your area and confirm they are appropriate and noninvasive before planting.
Hardscaping has the ability to transform an underused section of a lawn into a space for outdoor dining, seating, grilling, or entertaining. It also reduces the amount of grass you need to mow.

If you are replacing a larger lawn area with a patio or deck, you may need to temporarily store outdoor furniture, planters, and equipment to create a clearer work area. Since more than 45% of Public Storage properties offer drive-up access units that are helpful when loading larger household or outdoor items, you can find a location close by to help with your landscape redesign.

Decorative gravel, pebbles, river rock, and other landscaping stone can replace grass in areas where greenery is not a priority or light doesn’t reach to help vegetation grow. These materials can work well for pathways, borders, seating areas, and water-wise landscapes. Before covering a large area, consider drainage, local temperatures, weeds, and the overall climate. Artificial turf is another option that does not require mowing or irrigation for growth, though homeowners may want to consider surface temperature, drainage, installation cost, and long-term maintenance before installing.

A rain garden is a practical option if part of your yard regularly collects stormwater runoff. Rain gardens are shallow planted areas designed to temporarily collect and absorb runoff and typically include plants that can handle both wet and dry conditions. The right location, size, and plant selection depend on your yard’s drainage patterns, soil, and local climate.

Raised beds can turn part of a lawn into a dedicated area for growing vegetables, herbs, fruits, or flowers. They are not necessarily a low-maintenance alternative, since they still require watering and regular upkeep, but they can make outdoor space more useful.

Dirt, dust, food particles, and other debris can become embedded in rug fibers while a rug sits in storage. Clean your rug before you put it away, following the manufacturer’s cleaning instructions.
Vacuum both sides of the rug to remove loose dirt and dust. If it needs a deeper cleaning, have it professionally cleaned or use a cleaning method recommended for the rug’s material.

After cleaning your rug, give it plenty of time to dry before wrapping it up. This is one of the most important steps for preventing moisture damage. Lay the rug flat in a clean, well-ventilated area and allow both sides to dry. Depending on the material and cleaning method, this can take a while.
Don’t rush this step just because you’re ready to put the rug away. A rug that feels dry on the surface may still have moisture deeper in the fibers.
For most rugs, rolling is better than folding for long-term storage. Folding can create permanent creases, especially in rugs made from delicate or stiff materials.
Roll the rug tightly and evenly, with the pile facing inward when recommended by the manufacturer. Keep the roll as straight as possible, rather than letting it bend or become misshapen.
For valuable, antique, or handmade rugs, check with a professional rug cleaner or conservator for specific storage recommendations.
It may seem logical to wrap a rug in plastic to protect it from dirt and moisture, but plastic can trap moisture against the rug. That can create problems if any moisture remains in the fibers.

Instead, use a breathable fabric or rug storage cover that protects the rug from dust while allowing air to circulate. If you’re using a storage bag or cover, make sure it is large enough to fit the rolled rug without compressing it.
Don’t place a rolled rug directly on a concrete storage-unit floor. Keeping it elevated can help protect it from moisture and dirt.
Place the rug on a shelf, pallet, or another raised surface that can support its weight without damaging it. Make sure the storage method is stable and doesn’t risk the rug falling.

Don’t stack boxes, furniture, or other heavy belongings on top of a rolled rug. Heavy objects can compress the fibers or deform the rug, and moving those objects later can also make it harder to retrieve the rug without damaging it.

paragraphs: Most storage units start off neat but can end up as a jumble of “I’ll get to it later.” The good news? You can turn that clutter cave into a neatly packed space where everything has its place. Whether you’re stashing seasonal gear, putting away extra furniture, or just want to declutter your home, organizing your storage unit doesn’t have to be a hassle.

Before you start tossing things into your unit, map it out. Mentally divide the space into zones: furniture, seasonal items, hobby gear, and so on. Think of it like a tiny, walk-in closet—everything should have a home. Sketch a quick layout if that helps. Keep frequently used items near the front so you’re not climbing over holiday decorations to grab a lawn chair.

Don’t pick a unit that’s too small. If you have to pack everything wall-to-wall like a sardine can, you won’t be able to move, much less find anything later. Go for a unit that gives you room to grow, walk in, and access items without rearranging the whole thing.

Floor stacking is tempting. But adding a few budget-friendly shelving units can instantly tidy up the chaos and make use of vertical space. Shelves are perfect for storing bins, boxes, or anything that would otherwise end up buried at the bottom of a pile. Use clear plastic bins so you can see what’s inside—or go with labeled boxes if you want a cleaner look.
Pro tip: Label three sides of every bin for easy spotting, no matter where it’s placed.

Don’t just toss items in randomly. Heavy items go on the bottom, lighter ones on top. Stack boxes from largest to smallest, and keep similarly sized containers together to make stacking easier (and safer). If you’re storing furniture, use drawers and dressers to stash smaller items like linens or sports gear. To make more space, disassemble furniture like bed frames or tables and store the hardware in a labeled bag taped to the piece.

It’s tempting to fill every inch of the unit, but leave a small walkway down the middle. You’ll thank yourself when you need to grab something from the back without unpacking half the unit. That middle aisle is your backstage pass to everything you’ve stored. You can use an “L” or “U” shape for your aisle, just be sure to leave at least 12–18 inches of clearance at the front of your unit to open the door easily.

This sounds fancy, but a simple list on your phone will do. Jot down what you’ve stored and where. For example: “Green bin on top left shelf = winter clothes.” Not only will it save you digging time later, but it’ll also prevent you from buying duplicates of items you forgot you packed away. Before you seal up a box, take a quick photo of what’s inside. Then attach it to your digital list. You’ll never forget what “misc. tools” actually means again.

A well-organized unit isn’t just about being tidy, it’s about saving time, money, and stress. The better your system, the faster you’ll be in and out when you need something. And if you ever need to add more stuff, your future self will be grateful for the breathing room.

24/7 Security Operations Center
Our 24/7 Security Operations Center is a key part of our layered approach to security. Trained specialists continuously monitor camera feeds across our properties, providing real-time visibility and supporting our overall security program.

Our dedicated Loss Prevention professionals work behind the scenes every day to help reduce risk across our properties. Their responsibilities include fraud prevention, investigations, security technology management, risk analysis, and partnerships with local, regional, and national law enforcement agencies.

Well-lit storage facilities make it easier for customers to access their storage units while improving visibility throughout the property, especially during early morning or evening visits. Good lighting also helps staff and video surveillance systems monitor common areas more effectively and can discourage unwanted activity in darker spaces.

Perimeter fencing helps define the property boundary and direct access through designated entry points. When combined with features such as electronic gate access, video surveillance, and on-site management, perimeter fencing adds another layer to a facility's overall security program.

Video surveillance systems help monitor activity throughout a storage facility, including common areas such as entrances, exits, drive aisles, and other shared spaces. Cameras can support incident investigations, help deter unauthorized activity, and provide an additional layer of visibility across the property.
We've deployed more than 70,000 cameras across our properties as part of one of the industry's most comprehensive security monitoring programs. Camera placement and coverage vary by location.

Many of our locations use electronic gate access to help manage who enters and exits the property during designated access hours. Customers are typically assigned a unique access code, allowing only authorized individuals to enter the property. Controlled entry helps limit unauthorized access while providing a record of gate activity. Availability varies by location.

A self-storage facility is generally more secure when it uses multiple layers of security rather than relying on a single feature. Electronic gate access, video surveillance, quality locks, good lighting, perimeter fencing, and on-site management can work together to help discourage unauthorized access.

Security works in layers. That's why our approach extends beyond the features you see on the property. Behind them: a dedicated Loss Prevention team, a 24/7 Security Operations Center, and more than 70,000 cameras across our properties.

Whether you're storing household belongings during a move, business inventory, or seasonal items, check the security features at your location before you book. Every property lists its features online. Behind the scenes, our Loss Prevention team and 24/7 Security Operations Center support them all.
Facility features are only one part of protecting your belongings. The steps you take before and during storage can also help reduce risk.
Choose a high-quality disc lock or cylinder lock when available to help better secure your unit.
If your facility uses electronic gate access, avoid sharing your personal gate code with others.
Create a photo inventory of your stored items before moving them into your unit. This can be helpful for identification and insurance purposes.

paragraphs: Some things can be damaged by heat, humidity and cold. A climate-controlled unit may help keep your stuff within a set temperature or humidity range.
Need to stop by your storage unit on a regular basis? A climate-controlled unit may make sure your visit is comfortable in either hot or cold weather, year-round.

Some wines improve with age, but only under controlled conditions. Temperature swings and heat accelerate the wine's aging process, leaving it sharp, acidic and vinegary.
Warm, humid air can cause wood to swell and warp. Dry, cold winter air can make it shrink and crack. Neither extreme is good for wood furniture.
Mold and mildew thrive in warm, humid air. If either infest fabric, it can result in permanent damage.
Moisture and condensation are the enemies when it comes to photo gear and electronics. Camera bodies can corrode and lenses can be destroyed by humidity-loving fungi.
High heat and humidity can cause photos to curl, fade, and degrade rapidly. Climate control may keep your photos looking good for generations.
Heat easily melts LP records. Magnetic media like cassettes, tapes, and hard drives are sensitive to humidity and condensation.
Stringed instruments can warp and their glued joints can fail. Bacteria, mold, and mildew can grow in brasses and woodwinds. Pianos can suffer all these effects.

Storage Options for Every Vehicle Type
 Public Storage offers a variety of vehicle storage options, making it easier to find a space for a car, motorcycle, RV, trailer, or other wheeled equipment. Options range from outdoor parking spaces to covered spots and enclosed, ground-level storage units, offering flexibility based on how you plan to use the space.

Outdoor Parking Spaces
 Outdoor spaces are ideal for larger vehicles, work trucks, RVs, and trailers that don’t need
 full enclosure but still benefit from a dedicated, fenced area. These open-air spots provide easy
 access and can be a cost-effective solution for seasonal or frequent use.

Covered Parking Spots
 Covered vehicle storage spaces feature overhead protection that helps block direct sun exposure and
 moderate climate effects. This can help reduce wear on vehicle paint and interior materials compared
 with open-air parking.

Enclosed Vehicle Storage Units
 Enclosed storage units are ground-level spaces that function like a garage. These units can protect
 your vehicle from wind, rain, snow, and direct sunlight, which can be helpful when storing a vehicle
 for longer periods or preparing for a season of non-use.

Cars, Trucks, and Everyday Vehicles
 Standard cars, SUVs, and trucks fit comfortably in many vehicle storage options, including 20-foot
 enclosed units or covered parking spaces. Before reserving, it’s a good idea to measure your
 vehicle to confirm fit.

RVs, Campers, and Large Vehicles
 For larger vehicles, RVs, motor homes, and trailers, outdoor and covered spots provide ample room
 and flexibility. Many facilities can accommodate vehicles up to 50 feet long or more, though
 availability depends on location.

Motorcycles, ATVs, and Specialty Vehicles
 Smaller recreational vehicles such as motorcycles, ATVs, or specialty trailers can also be stored in
 dedicated vehicle storage spaces, including enclosed units where available.

Free Up Space at Home
 Storing vehicles offsite can help clear space in your driveway or garage, especially if you have
 multiple vehicles, limited parking, or seasonal equipment like boats or campers that don’t get
 daily use.

Flexible Month-to-Month Rentals
 Vehicle storage rentals are month-to-month, giving you the flexibility to keep your vehicle for as
 long or as short a time as you need without long-term commitments.

Seasonal Storage Use
 If you have seasonal vehicles like RVs, trailers, or summer-only cars, vehicle storage can provide a
 dedicated home during the off-season. This can make it easier to manage space year-round.

Maintenance Tips Before Storage
 Before you store a vehicle for any length of time, consider steps such as cleaning it, checking
 fluids, and ensuring your insurance is current. These practices help make sure your vehicle remains
 ready to drive when you retrieve it.

Frequently Asked Questions
 How Do I Know What Storage Type I Need?
 Choosing between outdoor, covered, and enclosed spaces depends on how long you plan to store your
 vehicle, local weather conditions, and how much protection you want from the elements. Enclosed
 spaces offer the highest level of protection, while outdoor spots are a flexible and accessible
 option.
